Gastric glands.description: Fundic gastric glands are tubular glands that open into the surface pits of the stomach. Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells release histamine that stimulates the parietal cells to make acid.
clinical: Autoimmune gastritis destroys the parietal cells in the body and fundus of the stomach, so less acid and intrinsic factor is made. Without intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed, which can cause pernicious anaemia.
A gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma) overstimulates the parietal cells, causing excess acid and recurrent peptic ulcers.

Muscularis externa.description: The muscularis externa is the muscle coat of the stomach wall, made of smooth muscle in three layers: an outer longitudinal layer, a middle circular layer and an inner oblique layer. Together they churn food and move it toward the pylorus.
clinical: Gastroparesis is delayed emptying of the stomach with no physical blockage, caused by weak or poorly coordinated contractions of the stomach wall, often from nerve damage. Diabetes is one of its most common causes, and it can cause nausea, bloating and feeling full early.

Mucosa.description: The mucosa is the innermost layer of the stomach wall. Its lamina propria is loose connective tissue that fills the space between the gastric glands, and the thin muscularis mucosae beneath it is a smooth muscle sheet that separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
clinical: A peptic ulcer is a break in the lining that extends through the muscularis mucosae, whereas an erosion stays above it. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID painkillers are the most common causes.

Enteric plexuses.description: The enteric nervous system is a network of nerve ganglia in the stomach wall that can coordinate movement and secretion largely on its own. The myenteric plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and controls their contractions, while the submucosal plexus sits in the submucosa and controls secretion and local blood flow.
clinical: Vagotomy, once used to treat peptic ulcers, cuts the vagus nerve fibres that feed the stomach's enteric nerve networks. It lowers acid output but can slow stomach emptying.

Serosa.description: The serosa is the outermost layer of the stomach wall: a thin connective tissue layer covered by mesothelium, the smooth lining of the peritoneal cavity. It lets the stomach slide smoothly against neighbouring organs.
clinical: A stomach ulcer that perforates through the serosa lets stomach contents spill into the abdomen, causing peritonitis, which is a surgical emergency.

Submucosa.description: The submucosa is a layer of connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscle coat. It carries the larger blood vessels, lymphatics and nerve networks of the stomach wall, and it lets the mucosa fold into the ridges called rugae.

Vessels.description: Arteries branch into a network in the submucosa that supplies the stomach wall. Submucosal veins drain blood toward the portal system, and lymphatic vessels carry lymph away from the wall.
clinical: In portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, the submucosal veins of the stomach can swell into varices that may bleed heavily.
Stomach cancer can spread through submucosal lymphatic vessels to nearby lymph nodes.

parts.description: Chief-rich gland bases are the deepest part of the fundic gastric glands, where chief cells are most numerous. Chief cells make pepsinogen, which acid converts into the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and gastric lipase, which starts fat digestion. In a stained section they show basophilic (blue-staining) cytoplasm from abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, with round nuclei near the base of the cell and pale apical granules.

Circular muscle bundles are the smooth muscle fibres that wrap around the stomach, running crosswise to its long axis. When they contract they narrow the stomach and help mix food and push it toward the pylorus. In a section, the circular fibres are cut across, so they look like small rings or dots, unlike the long streaks of the longitudinal layer.

The circular muscle layer is the middle smooth muscle coat of the muscularis externa, and it thickens at the pylorus to form the pyloric sphincter. The pyloric sphincter is a valve-like ring that controls the passage of chyme into the duodenum. Hypertrophy of this pyloric circular muscle causes hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a condition of infants that blocks the outlet of the stomach.

Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells are endocrine cells of the gastric glands, lying in the basal part of the fundic glands near the basement membrane. They release histamine, which stimulates neighbouring parietal cells to secrete acid, and their activity is driven by the hormone gastrin. In a stained section they are hard to pick out on routine staining, but silver stains or chromogranin A immunostaining reveal their granules.

The gland body is the main middle section of each fundic gland, lying between the narrow neck above and the base below. Its lining is mostly parietal cells, with chief cells towards the base and a few endocrine cells scattered among them. In a stained section, the body is recognised as the part of the gland tube packed with large pink cells.

The inner oblique muscle is the innermost of the three smooth muscle layers of the stomach wall, lying beneath the circular layer. Its fibres are incomplete, being best developed over the fundus and body and fading toward the pylorus. Because the fibres run diagonally, they are cut at many angles in a section, which helps tell this layer apart from the circular layer above.

The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue of the gastric mucosa that fills the spaces between the gastric glands. It holds fibroblasts, collagen and reticular fibres, plus lymphocytes, plasma cells and capillaries, and it supports the glands and carries blood and lymph vessels. In a stained section it is the pale, loosely arranged tissue between the tightly packed gland tubules.

The longitudinal bundles are the outermost smooth muscle fibres of the stomach, running lengthwise from the cardia (the upper part where the oesophagus joins) toward the pylorus. They are concentrated along the lesser and greater curvatures, and they continue from the longitudinal muscle of the oesophagus. In a section they appear as long, spindle-shaped streaks cut lengthwise along the outer edge of the muscle coat.

The middle circular muscle is the layer of smooth muscle lying between the outer longitudinal and inner oblique layers of the stomach. Its contraction narrows the stomach and propels food and chyme onward toward the pylorus. In a section, it is the middle of the three muscle bands, sitting between the longitudinal streaks outside and the oblique fibres inside.

Mucous neck cells line the narrow neck of each fundic gland, between the gastric pits and the parietal-rich body. They secrete a soluble, neutral mucus that coats and protects the gland lining. In a stained section they are pale, columnar cells with a flattened nucleus pushed to the base of the cell, and they stain less intensely than the parietal cells below.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin sheet of smooth muscle at the base of the mucosa, separating the lamina propria above from the submucosa below. Its contraction changes the shape of the mucosal folds and helps empty secretions from the gastric glands. In a stained section it appears as a thin pink band of spindle-shaped muscle nuclei lying just beneath the glands.

The myenteric connective tissue layer is a thin sheet of loose connective tissue between the outer longitudinal and middle circular muscle layers. It carries the small blood vessels and nerve fibres that supply both muscle layers and the myenteric plexus. In a stained section it appears as a pale strip of fibrous tissue between two bands of smooth muscle.

The myenteric connective tissue plane is the thin layer of loose connective tissue lying between the outer longitudinal and middle circular muscle layers of the stomach. It contains fibroblasts, collagen and small blood vessels, and the myenteric plexus ganglia sit within it, which makes it the place to find the nerve network between the two muscle layers. In a stained section it appears as a pale, fibrous band separating two bands of smooth muscle.

The myenteric plexus, also called Auerbach's plexus, is a network of enteric ganglia and nerve fibres lying between the outer longitudinal and middle circular muscle layers. It controls the rhythm and strength of contractions in both muscle layers, so it drives peristalsis and mixing in the stomach. In a stained section, look for small clusters of nerve cells with large pale nuclei within the connective tissue between the two muscle layers.

Oblique bundles are the deepest smooth muscle fibres of the stomach, lying against the submucosa beneath the circular layer. Their diagonal course gives a twisting, squeezing action that helps churn and mix food with gastric juice, and in a section they are told apart from the circular fibres by their slanted orientation.

The outer longitudinal muscle is the outermost smooth muscle layer of the stomach, lying directly beneath the serosa. Its fibres shorten the stomach along its length and help the organ empty. It is separated from the middle circular layer by a thin connective tissue sheet that carries the myenteric plexus.

Parietal cells are large, rounded cells in the neck and body of the fundic glands that secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Acid is made by a proton pump in their secretory canaliculi, and intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum. In a stained section they are deeply eosinophilic (pink) with a central round nucleus, and they bulge outwards from the gland wall. Loss of these cells in autoimmune gastritis leads to pernicious anaemia.

The nuclei of the gastric gland epithelial cells are the round to oval, blue-staining control centres of these cells, each holding DNA and one or more nucleoli, the small dense bodies where ribosomes are made. Their position depends on cell type: they sit centrally in parietal cells, near the base in chief cells, and flattened at the base of mucous neck cells. In a stained section, use these positions to work out which gland cell type you are looking at.

The submucosal artery is a branch of the gastric arteries that forms a network in the submucosa, the layer beneath the mucosa. Its branches supply the submucosa and mucosa, and send arterioles through the muscle coat to feed the muscle layers. In a section it is a round, thick-walled vessel whose muscular wall is thicker than that of the accompanying vein, which is thin-walled and often collapsed.

Submucosal lymphatics are thin-walled vessels in the submucosa that collect lymph from the mucosa and the muscle coat. They form a plexus that drains toward regional lymph nodes along the lesser and greater curvatures of the stomach. In a stained section they look pale or empty, with a thin wall and no red blood cells in the lumen.

The submucosal plexus, also called Meissner's plexus, is a network of enteric ganglia and nerve fibres lying in the submucosa, next to the inner border of the circular muscle. It controls gastric secretion and the blood flow to the mucosa and submucosa. In a stained section, look for small ganglia in the submucosal connective tissue, usually close to the submucosal arterioles.

The submucosal vein is a thin-walled vein in the submucosa that drains blood from the stomach wall into the gastric veins. These veins empty into the portal venous system, so blood from the stomach passes through the liver. In a stained section it has a wide, often collapsed lumen and a thin wall, and it lies beside the thicker-walled submucosal artery.

The surface and gastric pit epithelium is the single layer of tall mucous cells that lines the stomach's inner surface and the gastric pits, the openings into the fundic glands. These cells secrete an alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus that forms a protective gel against acid and pepsin. In a stained section, look for tall columnar cells with pale, mucus-filled apical cytoplasm and basal nuclei, lining the surface and the pits.
